draw.question: Up to how long an outage does this guide prepare a household for?
draw.expectedAnswer: up to seventy-two hours

draw.question: What climate is the guide written for, and what does it assume about a generator?
draw.expectedAnswer: a temperate climate and assumes no backup generator

draw.question: In what order should the sections be worked through, and which matter most?
draw.expectedAnswer: Work through the sections in order; the earlier sections cover the preparations that matter most

draw.question: How much water should be stored per person per day, and how much per person over the full period?
draw.expectedAnswer: four litres of water per person per day, which means twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours

draw.question: How is the water allowance split?
draw.expectedAnswer: Half of that allowance is for drinking, and the other half covers cooking and basic hygiene

draw.question: What kind of containers, storage condition, and replacement interval apply to stored water?
draw.expectedAnswer: food-grade containers, keep the containers out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months

draw.question: If a storm is forecast, what extra water source should you fill, and what is that water for (and not for)?
draw.expectedAnswer: also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking

draw.question: How many days of non-perishable food should the dedicated shelf hold?
draw.expectedAnswer: non-perishable food sufficient for three days

draw.question: Name the good non-perishable food choices listed.
draw.expectedAnswer: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk

draw.question: What kind of can opener must you own, and why not an electric one?
draw.expectedAnswer: a manual can opener, because an electric one will be useless

draw.question: In what order should you eat food during the outage?
draw.expectedAnswer: Eat the perishable food from the refrigerator first, then the food from the freezer, and only then open the emergency shelf

draw.question: About how long does an unopened refrigerator keep food safe?
draw.expectedAnswer: about four hours

draw.question: About how long does a full freezer hold a safe temperature versus a half-full one?
draw.expectedAnswer: about forty-eight hours, but a half-full freezer holds it for only about twenty-four hours

draw.question: What should you do with the fridge and freezer doors, and what reminder should you add?
draw.expectedAnswer: Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a note to each door as a reminder

draw.question: Perishable food that has spent more than how long above what temperature should be discarded?
draw.expectedAnswer: more than two hours above four degrees Celsius should be discarded

draw.question: What should be your primary light source, and what should you avoid, and why?
draw.expectedAnswer: battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light source, and avoid candles entirely, since candles are a leading cause of house fires during outages

draw.question: How many lights per person and how many spare battery sets per light should you store?
draw.expectedAnswer: at least one light per person, plus two spare sets of batteries for each light

draw.question: Where should a headlamp and a lantern be kept?
draw.expectedAnswer: one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen

draw.question: Where must you never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator, and why?
draw.expectedAnswer: Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window, because each of these produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal

draw.question: How many carbon monoxide alarms, of what type, on which floors?
draw.expectedAnswer: at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep

draw.question: In cold weather, which room should you gather in, and what beats an improvised heater?
draw.expectedAnswer: one small room on a south-facing side of the home ... layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater

draw.question: Below what indoor temperature, if you cannot stay warm, should you relocate, and to where?
draw.expectedAnswer: below ten degrees Celsius ... relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home

draw.question: What kind of radio should you keep, and what should you know beforehand?
draw.expectedAnswer: a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and know the frequency of your local emergency station before the outage begins

draw.question: How many times does a full twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour power bank recharge a typical phone?
draw.expectedAnswer: a full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours will recharge a typical phone roughly four times

draw.question: What phone mode and contact arrangement should you set, and why texts?
draw.expectedAnswer: low-power mode at the start ... one out-of-area contact whom every member of the household will text, because text messages get through congested networks more reliably than voice calls

draw.question: How many days' supply of prescription medication should you keep, plus what kit?
draw.expectedAnswer: a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication

draw.question: Up to how many days does refrigerated medication like insulin remain usable at room temperature, and whom should you confirm with?
draw.expectedAnswer: up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist

draw.question: Whose phone numbers should you write on paper, and why?
draw.expectedAnswer: the phone numbers of your pharmacy, your doctor, and the poison-control line on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book

draw.question: How long should you wait before switching major appliances back on, and why?
draw.expectedAnswer: Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise

draw.question: What sign in the freezer means food can be safely refrozen?
draw.expectedAnswer: if food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen

draw.question: Within what time should you restock what was used, starting with what?
draw.expectedAnswer: within one week, starting with water and batteries

draw.question: What note should you write afterward, and what should you fix before the next outage?
draw.expectedAnswer: write a one-page note about what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one of those gaps before the next outage arrives

ORIGINAL GUIDE FACT CENSUS (F1..F32), body sentences split on . ! ? in order:
F1: This guide explains how to prepare an ordinary household to manage safely and comfortably through a power outage lasting up to seventy-two hours.
F2: It is written for a temperate climate and assumes no backup generator.
F3: Work through the sections in order; the earlier sections cover the preparations that matter most.
F4: Store four litres of water per person per day, which means twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours.
F5: Half of that allowance is for drinking, and the other half covers cooking and basic hygiene.
F6: Store the water in food-grade containers, keep the containers out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months.
F7: If a storm is forecast and you have advance warning, also fill the bathtub; bathtub water is for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking.
F8: Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food sufficient for three days.
F9: Good choices are canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk.
F10: Choose foods that require no cooking, and make sure you own a manual can opener, because an electric one will be useless.
F11: Eat the perishable food from the refrigerator first, then the food from the freezer, and only then open the emergency shelf.
F12: An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe for about four hours.
F13: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about forty-eight hours, but a half-full freezer holds it for only about twenty-four hours, so it is worth keeping the freezer consolidated and full, even if some of the space is taken up by containers of frozen water.
F14: Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a note to each door as a reminder.
F15: Any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius should be discarded; when in doubt, throw it out.
F16: Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light source, and avoid candles entirely, since candles are a leading cause of house fires during outages.
F17: Store at least one light per person, plus two spare sets of batteries for each light.
F18: Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, and place them where they can be found in the dark.
F19: Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window, because each of these produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal.
F20: Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.
F21: In cold weather, choose one small room on a south-facing side of the home, close its door, and gather everyone there; layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater.
F22: If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.
F23: Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and know the frequency of your local emergency station before the outage begins.
F24: Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours will recharge a typical phone roughly four times.
F25: Put your phone in low-power mode at the start of the outage, and agree in advance on one out-of-area contact whom every member of the household will text, because text messages get through congested networks more reliably than voice calls.
F26: Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, and rotate the medications so they stay in date.
F27: Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist before an emergency happens.
F28: Write down the phone numbers of your pharmacy, your doctor, and the poison-control line on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.
F29: Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise.
F30: Check the freezer: if food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen.
F31: Restock everything used during the outage within one week, starting with water and batteries.
F32: Finally, write a one-page note about what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one of those gaps before the next outage arrives.
